result.keyword: how to train for a first marathon

items.markdown:
Training for your first marathon is an exciting milestone. Most beginner plans span **16 to 20 weeks** , assuming you can already comfortably run/walk or run about 3 to 5 miles at a time and maintain a baseline of 15–20 miles per week.

#### Phase 1: The Building Blocks (Weeks 1–4)

- **Weekly Mileage:** Start around 15–20 miles total.
- **Easy Runs (3–4 miles):** Run at a conversational pace. If you can't talk in full sentences, you're going too fast.
- **The Long Run (6–8 miles):** Usually done on the weekend. Build this up slowly by no more than 10% per week.
- **Strength & Mobility (2 days):** Focus on glutes, core, hips, and single-leg stability to keep injury away.

#### Phase 2: Building Endurance (Weeks 5–12)

- **Weekly Mileage:** Gradually scale up to 25–40 miles per week.
- **Pace Variation:** Introduce tempo runs or race-pace miles into one of your midweek sessions.
- **Peak Long Run:** Work your way up to a 18-to-20-mile long run about 3 weeks before race day. (You don't need to run a full 26.2 miles in training; the taper will bridge the gap safely).
- **Fueling Practice:** Use your long runs to test out energy gels, sports drinks, and hydration gear. Never try anything new on race day.

#### Phase 3: The Taper (Weeks 13–16 / Final 3 Weeks)

- **Reduce Mileage:** Drop your weekly mileage by 20% to 50% so your muscles and glycogen stores can fully repair.
- **Rest & Sleep:** Prioritize high-quality sleep and easy stretching. You might feel "taper madness"—phantom aches and restless energy—which is totally normal.
- **Race Day:** Line up with confidence, pace yourself conservatively for the first half (13.1 miles), and run your own race.

#### Golden Rules for Beginners

**80/20 Rule:** About 80% of your runs should feel easy and slow; only 20% should feel hard or fast.
1. **Listen to Your Body:** Distinguish between normal muscle fatigue and sharp, persistent joint pain. Rest a day early rather than being forced to rest a month late.
2. **Gear Check:** Get properly fitted for running shoes at a local specialty shop, and replace them if they have more than 300–500 miles on them before the race.
3. **Follow Structured Plans:** Look into trusted blueprints like the Every Woman's Marathon Beginner Plan[Every Woman's Marathon Beginner Plan](https://everywomansmarathon.com/training/beginner-marathon-plan/) or classic programs from Hal Higdon[Hal Higdon](https://www.halhigdon.com/) or RRCA[RRCA](https://www.rrca.org/) to map out your calendar day-by-day.[[1]](https://everywomansmarathon.com/training/beginner-marathon-plan/)

To help tailor a plan for you, tell me:

- What is your **current weekly mileage** or longest recent run?
- Do you have a **target race date** in mind?
